Profile errors are mean relative $L_{2}$ errors (%) as in Fig. 2; the statistical errors of the MD profiles are about 1%. “Quarter” denotes training on a quarter of the runs. Means exclude failed solutions (footnotes). Entries in parentheses are errors of the final iterates of Euler–Lagrange iterations that mostly did not converge (footnote $c$). Structural checks give maxima on the MD profiles of the ions: relative net internal force, Hessian asymmetry and path dependence of the free energy ( Supplementary Information, section S4.3).

plain.summary: The study addresses the challenge of accurately modeling the behavior of ionic systems within a specific material context, aiming for a balance between detailed molecular information and broader applicability. A novel neural density functional is constructed, incorporating physical constraints to ensure consistency with known laws and symmetries. The resulting functional demonstrates improved predictive capabilities compared to existing methods, particularly in capturing complex correlations and transferring spatial information, and requires significantly less training data. This approach seeks to bridge the gap between atomistic simulations and macroscopic continuum models.

fulltext.summary: The work addresses the development of a neural density functional to model the behavior of electrolytes, focusing on preserving key physical symmetries and thermodynamic properties. The functional is trained using force matching, weighting bins inversely proportional to the variance of molecular dynamics estimates and compensating for a suppression factor in the force density. The resulting functional demonstrates improved accuracy compared to alternative architectures, achieving errors of 1.50% and 3.11% for ion profiles at specific dielectric constants, and maintains this accuracy even when trained on only a quarter of the available data.

items.title: Variational Derivation of the Weak Form for Viscous Flows Involving Free Surfaces with Implications for Geodynamic Simulations
items.abstract: Geodynamic simulations involve solving the Stokes equations, where boundary conditions play a crucial role in governing internal dynamics and surface topography evolution. A common approach is to model the interface in contact with air as a free surface. This interface is stress-free and deforms in response to internal force balances, which is essential for understanding processes ranging from rifted margins to subduction. However, a free surface can introduce instabilities and oscillations in the numerical solution, commonly known as the "drunken sailor" instability, forcing the use of small time steps. Geodynamic models therefore often employ stabilization terms based on the gravitational effect of free-surface motion. To date, these terms have been derived primarily on a heuristic basis. Here, we apply variational calculus to the energy-minimization formulation of incompressible Stokes flow. Using the Gateaux derivative, we derive the complete weak form for a deforming free-surface domain and show that the stabilization terms arise naturally from the free-surface assumption. We consider the linear-viscosity case and identify two boundary-integral contributions: one associated with internal viscous deformation and the other with gravitational body force. Two benchmark cases demonstrate the consistency of the derived formulation with previously proposed stabilization approaches. Our results provide a mathematical foundation for the commonly used gravity stabilization and identify an additional viscous boundary contribution.
excerpts: [6 Numerical Test Cases] Two test cases are considered to assess the accuracy, stability, and applicability of the proposed free-surface stabilization formulations. The tests are arranged in increasing order of physical and numerical complexity. The first case is the Rayleigh–Taylor benchmark and the second test is the Rising Plume test.

[7 Results] Caption: Figure 5: Mean Absolute Error (MAE), defined by Equation ( 70), for the upper surface of the Rayleigh–Taylor instability. The MAE is compared for both full and gravity - only stabilization methods across various time steps and lid viscosities. Both methods demonstrate consistent performance. As expected, the MAE is inversely proportional to lid rigidity, peaking at lower viscosity values where surface deformation is most significant. In the second case study, we examine the resulting topography for a lid viscosity of $\mu=10^{21}$ Pa $\cdot$ s and a time step of $dt=5000$ years. Figure 6 compares the fully stabilised, stabilised, and unstabilised simulations of the rising plume benchmark. Both stabilization methods yield results closely aligned with each other and accurately track the reference simulation ( $dt=100$ years).

[A.1 Numerical Workflow and ALE Time Integration] The numerical solution advances in time using an ALE formulation in which the physical velocity and the mesh velocity are treated as distinct quantities. At each time step, the Stokes problem is first solved on the current computational mesh. The resulting physical velocity is then used to determine the motion of selected mesh boundaries through a separate mesh-movement problem. The mesh coordinates are subsequently updated explicitly, and the resulting mesh quality is assessed before proceeding to the next time step. Let $t^{n}$ denote the current time and let $\Delta t^{n}$ be the time-step size. The computational state at time $t^{n}$ consists of the mesh coordinates, the physical fields, and the associated solver and function space definitions. The complete time-stepping procedure is summarized schematically in Algorithm 1. Caption: Algorithm 1 ALE time-stepping procedure

plain.summary: The study addresses challenges in simulating fluid flow with free surfaces, a common occurrence in geodynamic modeling. Researchers employed variational calculus and the Gateaux derivative to derive a weak form for incompressible Stokes flow, focusing on a deforming free-surface domain. The derivation revealed two boundary-integral contributions – one from viscous deformation and another from gravitational body force – providing a mathematical basis for stabilization techniques. Validation through benchmark cases confirmed the consistency of the derived formulation with existing methods and highlighted an additional viscous boundary contribution.

fulltext.summary: The study addresses the challenges of numerically simulating viscous flows with free surfaces, a common occurrence in geodynamic modeling. Researchers employed variational calculus and the Gateaux derivative to derive a weak form for incompressible Stokes flow, specifically focusing on a deforming free-surface domain. This derivation revealed stabilization terms arising naturally from the free-surface assumption, identifying both viscous boundary and gravitational body force contributions. The derived formulation was validated through two benchmark cases, the Rayleigh–Taylor instability and a rising plume, demonstrating consistency with existing stabilization approaches.

items.title: Symbolic-Permutation-Based Direct Sparse Jacobian Assembly for Accelerated Power-Flow Analysis
items.abstract: The repeated assembly of the sparse Jacobian matrix constitutes a primary computational bottleneck in the Newton-Raphson power-flow analysis. Through an algebraic equivariance analysis of the Jacobian matrix, this paper proposes a direct sparse Jacobian assembly method based on symbolic permutation. By pre-applying the permutation to the admittance matrix during a one-time symbolic phase, the runtime bus-type projection overhead is entirely eliminated. Consequently, complex Jacobian differentiation and global matrix assembly fuse into a single operation, yielding a single-pass, branchless algorithm that streams values directly into contiguous memory. The framework is realized in the open-source RustPower solver. Benchmarks on IEEE test systems and PEGASE 9241 demonstrate that the proposed assembly is 24.4-30.1x faster than the MATPOWER- style baseline and 6.0-7.8x faster than the Schafer-Braun optimized assembly. End-to-end, the grid-level solve time is 11.7x-154.3x faster than pandapower 3.5.4 with Numba, while leaving numerical results and convergence behavior unchanged. Compared with the native C++ LightSim2Grid 1.0.0, grid-level performance is comparable on IEEE 39 and 1.3x-1.8x faster on IEEE 118 and the PEGASE systems. The method extends directly to general problems where a sparse Jacobian inherits its structure from a static network operator, including transient stability analysis, EMT simulation, and OPF Hessian assembly.
excerpts: [II-B The Power-Flow Equation] Caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed method’s core innovation. By hoisting topology-dependent permutations offline via Theorem 1, the proposed framework eliminates runtime slicing and scattered writes, condensing the traditional loop into a single-pass direct-fill stream to achieve up to 21 $\times$ speedup and outperform the state-of-the-art open-source C++ solver.

[III-A Non-Holomorphic Deadlock and the Dual Real-Mapping Paradigm] Redundant Differentiation: Wasting significant CPU cycles and arithmetic throughput evaluating derivatives for dropped states (e.g., slack and PV bus voltage magnitudes) that are subsequently discarded. Indirect Spatial Partitioning: Relying on extensive layout-mapping tables to index and route derivatives into traditional $\bm{J}_{11}$ through $\bm{J}_{22}$ sub-blocks, introducing severe pointer-dereferencing and indirection overheads inside the iteration loop. Non-Contiguous Scatter Assembly: Enforcing dimensional reduction via scattered writes that distribute values across disjoint matrix segments, which completely disrupts hardware prefetching, invalidates CPU cache lines, and severely limits parallel scalability. These limitations transform the iteration hot path into a performance graveyard of branch mispredictions and cache invalidations, which also significantly lower the parallel efficiency on modern CPUs and GPUs.

[V-A Experimental Setup] Results are averaged over seven batches of 300 solves. We compare these paths against pandapower 3.5.4 with Numba [ 14 ] and LightSim2Grid 1.0.0 [ 15 ]. LightSim2Grid uses a C++ backend on a pre-built model. Given the rapid evolution of power-flow software, comparisons are performed using fixed software releases. The iteration loop timings in Table IV are averages of 20 repeated complete power-flow solves after warm-up, with initialized network models and cached solver data reused and the initial voltage reset for each solve.

plain.summary: The work addresses the significant computational cost associated with Jacobian matrix assembly in iterative optimization algorithms. A novel approach is presented that leverages symbolic permutation and algebraic equivariance to streamline the process, eliminating runtime overhead and fusing differentiation and assembly steps. The resulting algorithm demonstrates substantial speedups compared to existing methods, achieving significant reductions in solve times across various benchmark power systems. The technique's applicability extends beyond power-flow analysis to other network-based optimization problems.

fulltext.summary: The work addresses the computational expense of Jacobian matrix assembly within Newton-Raphson power-flow analysis, a process that traditionally involves repeated calculations and inefficient memory access patterns. The authors propose a novel approach based on symbolic permutation, pre-applying topological transformations to the admittance matrix to eliminate runtime overhead and consolidate differentiation and assembly into a single pass. This results in a branchless algorithm that directly streams values into contiguous memory, achieving significant speedups over existing methods, including a 11.7x-154.3x improvement in grid-level solve time compared to pandapower 3.5.4 with Numba. The framework was implemented in RustPower and validated on IEEE test systems and PEGASE 9241.

items.title: Linear and entropy-stable scheme for the dynamic van der Waals model of non-isothermal liquid-vapor flows
items.abstract: In this paper, we propose a linear and decoupled fully discrete scheme that preserves the entropy production property for the dynamic van der Waals model. This model provides a thermodynamically consistent diffuse-interface framework for describing non-isothermal phase transitions in single-component liquid-vapor systems, containing the coupled conservation laws of mass, momentum and energy. We first introduce an equivalent reformulation of the governing equations that avoids the use of chain-rule identities, which generally fail under discrete differentiation. Further, a component-wise convex-splitting method is employed to calculate the discrete chemical potential and temperature. This treatment provides a discrete entropy-stable inequality without a time step restriction. Based on the explicitly treated velocity, the scheme allows the three conservation equations to be solved linearly and sequentially in a decoupled manner. Since the momentum equation does not directly affect the entropy-stability analysis, we use a classical linear semi-implicit scheme to solve it. Numerical experiments verify the expected numerical accuracy. Simulations of droplet evaporation and two- and three-dimensional Leidenfrost effects further demonstrate the proposed method can capture complex non-isothermal phase-transition dynamics while numerically reproducing the discrete entropy production behavior.
excerpts: [2 The dimensionless equations] In order to improve numerical stability, reduce the difference among the physical scales, and simultaneously decrease the number of parameters, the governing equations are first non-dimensionalized. Before doing so, we adopt several assumptions commonly used in the literature [ 21, 35, 36 ]: (i) the shear and bulk viscosities are equal and proportional to the number density, [formula], where $\nu_{0}=\eta/\rho$ is the kinematic viscosity independent of $n$; (ii) the thermal conductivity is also proportional to the number density, $\lambda=k_{B}\nu_{0}n$; (iii) the gradient coefficient in energy is zero $K=0$ and $C$ is a positive constant, namely The viscosity and thermal conductivity coefficients can also be chosen to be either constants or nonlinear functions of the density and temperature. If the latter is adopted, the non-dimensionalization will be different.

[4.1 Convergence test] In this part, we use smooth initial data to test the convergence rates of the numerical scheme ( 32)-( 37), with no gravity ( $G=0$), on the isolated domain $\Omega=(0,L)^{2}$, where $L=100$ and $R=0.5$. The initial data are chosen to be trigonometric: Based on the decoupling property and the use of centered differences, the numerical algorithm is expected to be first-order accurate in time and second-order accurate in space. As the exact solution is unavailable, the Cauchy difference on adjacent grids is employed to calculate the temporal and spatial convergence orders, respectively. The definition is given as where $h_{f}$ denotes the numerical solution on the fine spatial (or temporal) mesh and $h_{c}$ is the one on the coarse spatial (or temporal) mesh. Here we set $h_{c}=2h_{f}$. In fact, $I_{c}^{f}$ is a bilinear projection, mapping the solution from fine grid to coarse grid. For the spatial order, we fix ${\Delta t}=0.01$ and change space step as $h=L/N$, [formula]. The Cauchy differences at final time $T_{final}=10$ and corresponding numerical convergence orders are presented in Tables 1, both of which are consistent with the expected results.

[5 Conclusion] A major feature of the proposed method is that it preserves the entropy-production law at the fully discrete level, which is one of the fundamental thermodynamic structures of the model. Numerical experiments verify the expected first-order temporal accuracy and second-order spatial accuracy and further demonstrate that the proposed method can effectively capture droplet evaporation, two- and three-dimensional Leidenfrost effects. These results indicate that the scheme is robust, efficient, and physically consistent. Future work will mainly focus on two directions. One is the generalization of the numerical scheme to complex models, such as thermodynamically consistent boundary conditions and multi-component flows. The other is the development of fully discrete schemes that simultaneously maintain entropy production and energy conservation, with additional attention to positivity preservation of density and temperature.

plain.summary: The study addresses the simulation of phase transitions in fluids by developing a numerical scheme for a specific thermodynamic model. Researchers reformulated governing equations and utilized a convex-splitting method to ensure entropy stability during discretization, avoiding issues with discrete differentiation. The resulting scheme allows for a decoupled, linear solution of conservation equations, with a classical approach used for the momentum equation. Validation through simulations of droplet evaporation and Leidenfrost effects demonstrates the scheme's ability to capture complex dynamics while maintaining numerical stability.

fulltext.summary: The work addresses the numerical simulation of phase transitions in liquid-vapor systems using a dynamic van der Waals model, which incorporates conservation laws for mass, momentum, and energy. To improve stability and reduce physical scale differences, the governing equations are non-dimensionalized and reformulated to avoid issues with discrete differentiation, and a component-wise convex-splitting method is used to calculate the chemical potential and temperature. The resulting scheme demonstrates first-order temporal accuracy and second-order spatial accuracy, as verified through convergence tests on a domain with dimensions 100x100, and successfully simulates phenomena like droplet evaporation and Leidenfrost effects.

items.title: Sustainable Cloud-Fog-Edge Systems for Smart Buildings: Algorithmic Adaptation under Memory Constraints and Dynamic Orchestration Strategies
items.abstract: The escalating environmental footprint of the Information and Communication Technol- ogy (ICT) sectorwith global Data Center electric- ity usage potentially reaching 3% by 2030 and the imperative for real-time responsiveness in smart buildings demand a foundational shift towards Edge Computing. This article proposes a holis- tic architectural and algorithmic approach for cre- ating autonomous, resilient, and privacy-preserving learning systems within smart buildings, advancing the core concept of the building itself as the data center. Our contributions, demonstrating originality compared to conventional centralized systems, are structured around three main pillars: 1) Validation of resilient data acquisition chains using the af- fordable Arduino ecosystem (Uno R4 WiFi/BME280) and secure persistence solutions including centralized archiving (Node-RED/MySQL) and secure remote transfer (Python/rsync/SSH). 2). The proposal of a lightweight, KOptim orchestration framework, inter- operable with the FIWARE standard, for the dynamic management of Service Level Agreements (SLA). 3) The adaptation and experimental valida- tion of the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm (GHA) for Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on low- power microcontrollers,We introduce and compare an iterative learning strategy using data buffers, featuring sorting and explicit preservation of extreme samples to maintain diversity. Experimental results on the high-dimensional Tour Perret sensor data confirm that this novel method, despite introducing a necessary temporal complexity of O(W log W ) due to sorting, achieves convergence and final result quality that is visually equivalent to processing the entire dataset in full memory, reliably identifying two distinct operational states.
excerpts: [IV-B Comparative Strategies for Limited Memory (Original Contribution)] To simulate the constrained environment of an embedded device (e.g., limited RAM) and allow the algorithm to process large datasets sequentially, we compared three learning strategies: Reference Method (Full Memory): Processing the entire dataset at once (infeasible on microcontrollers). Simple Block Processing: Iterative processing using fixed-size data buffers $W$ (e.g., 1024 lines). This simulates diversity by simply moving to a new block. Block Processing with Explicit Diversity Management (Proposed Method): This innovative strategy explicitly manages the buffer content to ensure diversity. The buffer is filled. The buffer is sorted (e.g., based on accMotion value), complexity $O(W\log W)$. Only samples at the extremities of the distribution (e.g., the lower and upper halves) are retained to maximize sample diversity. The resulting empty spaces are refilled with new data. The GHA step is executed on this diversified buffer.

[V-B K-MEANS Clustering for Activity Analysis] The differences between the results in C++ and Python programs can be attributed to several factors. The C++ program processes the data in blocks of 1024 rows, while the Python program processes the data sequentially. This may affect how the eigenvalues and eigenvectors are updated. The initial parameters, such as the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors, may be initialized differently in the two programs, which may influence the final results. The C++ program uses an online approach to update the eigenvalues and eigenvectors, while the Python program uses a batch approach. This may lead to differences in the convergence of the results. The Python program ignores rows without payload, which can reduce the number of data rows processed, while the C++ program does not seem to have this logic. The C++ program normalizes the data by ignoring some columns (1, 3, and 6), while the Python program normalizes all columns. This can lead to differences in the values of the processed data.

[VI-A Inherent Limitations of the Proposed Methodology] We detail the disadvantages and limitations of the proposed approach, as required by the critiques (Critique 2): PCA Linearity Limit: PCA (and GHA) is a linear method. It can only capture linear relationships between variables. If data relationships are non-linear, this method may not capture the true structure. Information Loss: Dimensionality reduction entails an inevitable loss of total variance. Implementation and Performance Cost: The explicit memory management strategy (sorting) increases the implementation complexity and the time complexity to $O(W\log W)$ per iteration, which affects speed on low-power devices. Dependency on Sorting Criterion: The success of the diversity preservation method relies heavily on choosing the correct variable for sorting (e.g., accMotion). A poor choice could compromise the preservation of diversity. Ecosystem Compatibility: There is a recognized time lag in algorithm development between microcontroller ecosystems (ARDUINO and Micropython).

plain.summary: The work addresses the challenges of deploying machine learning algorithms within resource-constrained environments, specifically focusing on smart building applications. Researchers developed a system utilizing low-power microcontrollers and a lightweight orchestration framework to manage data acquisition, storage, and processing. They adapted the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm for Principal Component Analysis, employing a data buffering strategy with sorting to achieve comparable results to full-memory processing while mitigating memory limitations.

fulltext.summary: The study investigates a method for processing large datasets on resource-constrained microcontrollers within a smart building environment. To address limited memory, a novel block processing strategy was developed that explicitly manages data diversity by sorting buffer contents and retaining extreme samples, resulting in a time complexity of O(W log W) per iteration. Experimental validation using Tour Perret sensor data demonstrated that this approach achieves comparable results to processing the entire dataset in full memory, reliably identifying two distinct operational states. The work also acknowledges limitations, including the method's reliance on linear relationships and the performance impact of the sorting step.

items.title: PDE-PFN: Prior-Data Fitted Neural PDE Solver
items.abstract: Motivated by the success of large language models (LLMs) with broad generalizability and robustness to noisy or unreliable pre-training data, we explore in-context prediction of PDE solution fields using approximate pre-training data. In addition, inspired by the posterior predictive mean-based inference mechanism of the in-context learning in prior-data fitted networks (PFNs), we propose PDE-PFN, a prior-data fitted neural solver that approximates the posterior predictive mean of PDE solutions via in-context learning. PDE-PFN builds on a PFN architecture with self- and cross-attention mechanisms of Transformer and is pre-trained on noisy approximate solutions generated by physics-informed neural networks, serving as diverse but not necessarily exact priors. Through experiments on a range of two-dimensional PDEs, we demonstrate that PDE-PFN achieves empirical generalization across heterogeneous equations, robustness under noisy priors, and zero-gradient-update in-context inference capability. PDE-PFN achieves competitive or improved predictive accuracy relative to the evaluated baselines while supporting flexible context and query representations.
excerpts: Caption: Figure 1: The overall workflow of PDE-PFN. Our model performs in-context learning (ICL) based on given observations (i.e., context) to infer solutions. At inference, PDE-PFN conditions on observations from the target instance without separate operator-level demonstrations or target-instance gradient updates. Even when trained with an approximated PINN prior, our method can improve over noisy approximate pretraining data.

[4.3 Cross-PDE Transfer after Fine-tuning] Caption: Table 5: The evaluation results for the operator learning task applied to CNSE. The best performance is marked in bold and the second-best performance is marked with underline. The experimental results in Table 5 show that both versions of our model outperform the baselines on two relative error metrics. Notably, although DPOT’s pre-training corpus already includes the CNSE dataset from PDEBench, our models still achieve superior performance over DPOT on both metrics. While DPOT was originally evaluated on predicting one time step ahead, in our setting the task was extended to predicting up to four time steps ahead. As a result, DPOT exhibited lower performance than reported in the original paper. These results support cross-PDE transfer after fine-tuning for multivariate trajectory prediction.

[H.3 Test-Time Prediction with Biased Context Noise in the 2D CDR Family] Since Theorem A.2 assumes unbiased noise, we further investigate how robust our model remains when the inference stage includes biased Gaussian noise added to the analytic solution. We set the standard deviation of Gaussian noise to $\sigma=0.01$ and vary only the magnitude of the bias. The evaluation is performed on the temporal extrapolation task of the 2D CDR equations, using the $L_{2}$ relative error for comparison. Caption: Table 10: The evaluation results for the temporal extrapolation tasks applied to the family of 2D CDR equations. They are measured at the seen coefficients ( [formula]). The experimental results in Table 10 show that when the bias is below 3%, the performance degradation remains relatively minor compared to the bias level. However, once the bias reaches approximately 3% or higher, the error begins to increase more noticeably. This indicates that PDE-PFN maintains robustness against moderate systematic bias, but large bias eventually leads to a degradation in accuracy as expected.

plain.summary: This work investigates a novel neural network architecture for solving partial differential equations, drawing inspiration from large language models and a specific inference mechanism called posterior predictive mean-based inference. The proposed method, PDE-PFN, utilizes a Transformer-based architecture pre-trained on solutions generated by physics-informed neural networks, which are treated as prior data. Experimental results demonstrate the model’s ability to generalize across different equations, maintain robustness with noisy data, and perform inference without gradient updates, ultimately achieving competitive predictive accuracy.

fulltext.summary: The study addresses the challenge of accurately solving partial differential equations (PDEs) by leveraging a novel neural network architecture termed PDE-PFN. This model utilizes a prior-data fitted network framework, incorporating self- and cross-attention mechanisms inspired by Transformer models, and is pre-trained on approximate solutions generated by physics-informed neural networks. Experiments on two-dimensional PDEs demonstrate the model's ability to generalize across different equations, maintain robustness with noisy data, and perform inference without gradient updates, achieving competitive or improved predictive accuracy compared to baseline methods. The model’s performance remains relatively stable when subjected to moderate systematic bias in the analytic solution, with a noticeable degradation in accuracy only when the bias exceeds approximately 3%.

items.title: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Automated Tuning of Specialized Neural Network Models
items.abstract: Many machine learning approaches are two-level: an expert selects a class of methods, within this class the choice of key components is critical and usually manual. This paper addresses the automatic tuning of these components and proposes a framework transferable across models of different nature. The multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework has three roles---analyst, coder, and recorder~---with an experiment log and a sandboxed execution environment. Unlike systems that optimize the entire ML script or search architectures in a discrete space, the framework operates over an open but semantically narrow space: the agent generates code only for the specified components, leaving the overall network structure unchanged. The approach is validated in two directions: tuning a classification spiking neural network with correlation learning, and solving high-order differential equations with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINN). Across five tasks---spiking classification on MNIST and Digits, and boundary-value problems for the generalized nonlinear Schrödinger equation (GNLSE) and Kuramoto--Sivashinsky (KS) equations---the agent outperforms the baselines: classification accuracy is 13 percentage points (MNIST) and 6 percentage points (Digits) higher; the error against the analytical single-soliton solution is reduced approximately 2491-fold; the invariant-preservation error drops approximately 325-fold in the selected GNLSE run with a Gaussian perturbation and by more than 100-fold on average over repeated initializations; and the mass drift drops 14-fold for the KS problem with a Gaussian perturbation. The framework thus tunes key components on tasks of different nature without changing its internal structure.

plain.summary: The study investigates a method for automating the optimization of specific components within machine learning models, moving beyond full script optimization or discrete architectural searches. A multi-agent large language model system is developed, assigning roles for analysis, code generation, and record-keeping within a controlled environment. The framework demonstrates improved performance across various tasks, including solving high-order differential equations using a particular type of neural network, with significant reductions in error and drift observed.

The system employs an "analyst," "coder," and "recorder" to systematically explore a semantically narrow space of potential modifications, leaving the overall network architecture unchanged. This approach was tested on tasks including tuning a classification spiking neural network and solving high-order differential equations using Physics-Informed Neural Networks, demonstrating improved classification accuracy and error reduction compared to baseline methods. The framework's limitations include a restricted search space, preventing structural transformations beyond a predefined catalogue of editable blocks.

items.title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective
items.abstract: Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom ($Re$) and the degree of non-equilibrium ($SK/ε$). By applying Weaver's well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.
excerpts: [2 Turbulence Through the Lens of Complexity] By explicitly distinguishing the disorganized stochastic regime (Regime II) from structurally emergent dynamics (Regime IV), this taxonomy demystifies the generalization crisis in data-driven turbulence modeling. It demonstrates that ML-RANS failures in complex flows are not caused by algorithmic limitations or insufficient training data, but by the fundamental misapplication of statistical tools to structurally emergent regimes where non-Markovian memory effects physically invalidate local closure.

The challenge in Regime IV is not insufficient data, but the impossibility of learning a universal mapping for a highly flow-specific, emergent quantity. Consequently, the most robust strategy is not to model this history dependence, but to dynamically resolve the memory-bearing coherent structures via scale-resolving simulations (SRS).

Researchers developed a turbulence taxonomy map using a complexity framework, classifying flows based on Reynolds number and non-equilibrium parameters. This classification aims to guide the appropriate application of different AI/ML techniques, including physics-informed neural networks, to maximize effectiveness and avoid misapplication.

fulltext.summary: The study addresses the limitations of applying machine learning techniques to turbulence modeling, particularly the issue of generalization across different flow regimes. The authors propose a turbulence taxonomy map based on Reynolds number and the ratio of shear to dissipation rates, classifying flows into regimes where data-driven models struggle due to non-Markovian memory effects. They argue that statistical learning methods, like those used in ML-RANS, are inherently limited in their ability to accurately represent complex, emergent flow structures, leading to irreducible Bayes error and poor performance when applied outside their training domain. Ultimately, the work suggests that physics-informed neural networks are most effective in specific regimes within this taxonomy.

items.title: PINNs for N=2* holography
items.abstract: Can a holographic theory be reconstructed from its equation of state? We investigate this question using physics-informed neural networks in the bosonic-mass sector of the Pilch--Warner model. We first validate the PINN approach against an analytic solution encoding the leading high-temperature corrections to the conformal equation of state. We then reconstruct nonlinear black-brane geometries and the scalar potential using thermodynamics, ultraviolet asymptotics, Ward identities, and horizon regularity. Independent solutions of the bulk Einstein-scalar equations demonstrate that accurately reproducing thermodynamics with a trained PINN does not guarantee an accurate reconstruction of the scalar potential. High-precision knowledge of the high-temperature equation of state constrains nonlinear interactions in the bulk scalar potential. Fixing the cubic coupling to its exact PW value, motivated by this high-temperature extraction, reduces the maximum sampled error in the reconstructed scalar self-interactions by a factor of $\sim 15$ compared with constraining only the bulk scalar mass. Adding knowledge of the bulk viscosity of the gauge theory plasma further reduces this error by an additional factor of $\sim 13$, with independent forward solutions reproducing the bulk viscosity within $0.09\%$.

Researchers employed a neural network architecture trained to satisfy governing equations and validated it against a known analytical solution. The investigation then focused on reconstructing geometric properties and potential energy functions, revealing that thermodynamic accuracy does not always translate to accurate reconstruction of all physical parameters. Incorporating additional constraints, such as viscosity, significantly improved the precision of the reconstructed parameters.

items.title: Physics-informed random neural architectures on compact boundaryless multiply connected manifolds for random-operator models in machine learning and uncertainty quantification
items.abstract: We introduce stochastic physics-informed neural networks (SPINNs) for stochastic boundary-value problems (SBVPs) with random operators. The method enforces physics through a structural probabilistic coupling: a common Gaussian stochastic germ drives both the SBVP random operator and a manifold-based stochastic neural architecture. The stochastic neural network is non-feedforward and intrinsically random. A latent Gaussian field and an inhomogeneous Poisson point process on a compact, boundaryless, multiply connected manifold generate random neuron locations, geodesically local sparse connectivity, and a sparse random weight matrix, all governed by a low-dimensional hyperparameter. For deterministic inputs, the network output is random and can represent non-Gaussian random operators. Training is performed in observation space: SBVP simulations produce random observables, while the SNN defines a predictive conditional probability density function. The supervised objective combines data fidelity, through negative log-likelihood, with a cross-entropy alignment term relative to the SBVP-induced conditional distribution. The resulting target is a convex mixture of observation-induced and SBVP-induced distributions, with a dimensionless parameter controlling robustness to model--data mismatch. The shared stochastic germ yields common-random-numbers Monte Carlo estimators and reduced-variance gradients. The method uses only evaluations of the SBVP solution mapping, without differentiating or modifying it, and avoids PDE-residual or boundary-penalty losses. A stochastic elliptic problem on a periodic cylindrical surface illustrates the approach in SBVP-consistent and SBVP-misspecified regimes. A generalized-posterior formulation is also outlined for hyperparameter inference and posterior averaging without per-query reoptimization.

The authors propose a novel framework using stochastic physics-informed neural networks (SPINNs) that incorporates randomness in both the operator and the network architecture, driven by a shared stochastic process. The network’s structure is defined by a latent Gaussian field and a Poisson point process on a manifold, resulting in a non-feedforward architecture with sparse connectivity and random weights, trained using a combination of data fidelity and distribution alignment.

The method trains the network in observation space, using negative log-likelihood and cross-entropy alignment to compare the network's predictive conditional probability density function with the SBVP-induced conditional distribution, and in a misspecified regime, the SNN incurs about a [formula] larger CRPS than a data-driven benchmark. items.title: Metric-Driven Reinforcement Learning for Object Hallucination Reduction in LVLM-Based Image Captioning
items.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have excelled in joint visual and language understanding, particularly in image captioning. However, LVLMs remain prone to object hallucination, describing non-existent entities in the given image. Previous remedies, including dataset-enhanced supervised training and reinforcement learning from human feedback, show promise but rely heavily on costly human involvement, limiting scalability. To address this, we propose a reinforcement learning framework to mitigate object hallucination in LVLM-based image captioning, driven entirely by natural language processing (NLP) metrics. While optimizing reinforcement learning solely on NLP metrics offers scalability, it also introduces pitfalls: reward hacking, sparse feedback, and costly training. Our framework sidesteps these by introducing an Object Consistency Score (OCS) capturing both correctness and coverage of objects, incorporating KL-regularization for denser token-level guidance, and designing a lightweight PPO variant that fine-tunes adapters atop a frozen LVLM backbone, achieving efficiency and stability. Extensive experiments on the InstructBLIP baseline demonstrate the effectiveness and generalizability of our framework, achieving a substantial hallucination reduction of up to 41\% on the COCO dataset and 29\% on the Visual Genome. Furthermore, the framework can enhance caption quality by incorporating complementary evaluation metrics such as BERTScore and METEOR. These results reveal a broader insight in multimodal learning: LVLMs can effectively self-correct hallucinations using metric feedback, motivating deeper exploration into scalable reinforcement frameworks that significantly reduce human effort.
excerpts: [I Introduction] The remaining sections are organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 details our proposed methodology, including the formulation of the Markov Decision Process (MDP) for image captioning, the design of the reward function, and the modeling of reinforcement learning networks, followed by fine-tuning the model through solving the MDP with RL. Section 4 presents the experimental results, and Section 5 reports the ablation studies. Section 6 provides discussions, while Section 7 concludes the paper and outlines directions for future research.

[IV-B Experimental Results] Additionally, our method is able to maintain or enhance caption quality across various metrics. Table III presents our results. The row Ours demonstrates the use of OCS and KL divergence, maintaining performance comparable to the base model, InstructBLIP. There is a slight increase in SPICE, BLUE, and BERTScore, which we attribute to the generated captions being more factual, concise, and focused, resulting in shorter and more precise outputs. When ground truth captions are available, incorporating METEOR and BERTScore, as in Ours+, significantly improves caption quality. It is evident that Ours+ significantly improves captioning performance across SPICE, BLEU, and BERTScore, surpassing all previous baselines. Extend evaluations to more complex dataset: We evaluate our model on the Visual Genome dataset using the CCEval metric from Halle-switch [ 91 ] to assess its performance in more complex settings with denser object in the image.

[VII Limitations and Future Directions] While our framework effectively mitigates object hallucination, several limitations remain. First, OCS is currently defined over object sets and therefore primarily targets object-level hallucination. Hallucinations involving incorrect attributes (e.g., color) or relations (e.g., spatial or interaction errors) are not explicitly optimized. However, since OCS is fundamentally a precision–recall (F1-based) formulation, it can be extended to structured units such as (object, attribute) pairs or (subject, relation, object) triplets, provided reliable automatic extraction is available. Exploring such extensions is an important direction for future work. Second, in real-world deployment settings where ground-truth annotations are unavailable, hallucination mitigation depends on the coverage and accuracy of the object detector used to construct visual object sets. Detectors limited to fixed vocabularies (e.g., COCO’s 80 classes) may leave non-COCO hallucinations undetected. Integrating open-vocabulary detection models could further improve robustness in real-world applications.

plain.summary: The study investigates a method for improving the accuracy of image captioning models, which sometimes fabricate objects not present in the image. Researchers developed a reinforcement learning approach that uses automated language metrics to guide the model's learning process, reducing the need for human intervention. This framework incorporates a novel consistency score and regularization techniques to prevent undesirable behaviors and improve training efficiency, ultimately leading to a significant reduction in hallucinated objects across multiple datasets. The findings suggest that models can be refined through automated feedback, potentially opening avenues for more scalable training methods.

fulltext.summary: The paper addresses the problem of object hallucination in image captioning models, specifically within Large Vision-Language Models. To mitigate this, the authors propose a reinforcement learning framework that utilizes natural language processing metrics, such as an Object Consistency Score and KL-regularization, to guide the fine-tuning of adapters on a frozen LVLM backbone. Experimental results on the COCO and Visual Genome datasets demonstrate a substantial reduction in hallucination, up to 41% and 29% respectively, while also maintaining or improving caption quality as measured by metrics like BERTScore and METEOR.

items.title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds
items.abstract: Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of continuous-time dynamical systems provide rich structure for statistical learning. A central challenge is how to integrate data with PDE constraints in a principled way to improve generalization. In this paper, we characterize the statistical estimation and generalization properties of learning solutions to the heat equation with a noisy source function from finite, randomly sampled data. We first derive a novel variational formulation, which we characterize as the minimizer of loss function for an energy regularized and ellipticity debiased Sobolev regression. By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}---samples of the source function of the heat equation---to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.

Researchers developed a variational formulation that combines data with PDE constraints, utilizing energy regularization and debiasing techniques to improve generalization. items.title: AI-Assisted Tumor-Growth Law Discovery from Sparse Data: Refitting and LLM-Based Ranking
items.abstract: Inferring tumor-growth laws from sparse, noisy observations requires more than accurate curve fitting. We study an AI-assisted workflow involving symbolic regression, mathematical admissibility checks, coefficient refitting, and large language model (LLM) ranking. Synthetic Gompertz data allow trajectory fit, forecasting, and recovery of the governing growth law to be assessed separately. A dense noiseless control recovers the generating family, but sparse noisy sampling frequently leads to alternative forms. Among retained candidates in the tested configurations, physics-informed neural network refitting often increases growth-law error, whereas classical nonlinear least squares usually reduces it. A separate exploratory analysis of archived LLM rankings shows no consistent improvement over selection by training error and identifies errors in mathematical reasoning. Plausible saturation, accurate trajectory fits, and convincing explanations can therefore coexist with incorrect growth laws. Mathematical validity and law recovery require evaluation alongside predictive performance.

It withholds the generating equation and parameters, future volumes, forecast errors, and law-level errors. plain.summary: The study addresses the challenge of extracting accurate mathematical models from limited and imperfect data representing tumor growth. Researchers developed a process combining symbolic regression, refinement steps, and LLM ranking to identify potential growth laws. The investigation found that while neural network-based refinement sometimes worsened model accuracy, traditional optimization methods often improved it, highlighting the importance of considering multiple evaluation criteria beyond predictive power.

fulltext.summary: The study addresses the challenge of discovering accurate tumor-growth laws from limited and imperfect data. Researchers developed an AI-assisted workflow combining symbolic regression, mathematical checks, coefficient refitting using both classical and physics-informed neural network methods, and large language model ranking. Experiments using synthetic Gompertz data revealed that while physics-informed neural network refitting sometimes worsened growth-law error, classical nonlinear least squares typically improved it, and LLM rankings did not consistently outperform selection based on training error. The analysis highlights the potential for plausible explanations and accurate predictions to coexist with incorrect underlying growth laws.

items.title: Targeted Entropy-Stable Nonlinear Artificial Dissipation for High-Order Spectral-Element Summation-By-Parts Discretizations
items.abstract: Artificial dissipation improves the robustness of high-order methods for under-resolved flows, but can compromise accuracy and suppress physically relevant structures if its strength and spatial distribution are not appropriately controlled. We present a sensor-activated nonlinear artificial-dissipation framework, inspired by the residual correction method, for continuous and discontinuous summation-by-parts discretizations. In contrast to many existing spectral-element dissipation operators that either reduce the formal order of accuracy or target only the highest polynomial modes, the proposed framework permits design- and higher-order dissipation with explicit control over its magnitude, spatial distribution, activation, and convergence rate under mesh refinement. This modular construction also recovers several existing methods through appropriate choices of its components. The dissipation preserves discrete conservation and semidiscrete entropy stability whenever the base method satisfies these properties. It is dimensionally consistent, element local, and discretization agnostic, as the added term is constructed independently of the base spatial residual. For smooth solutions under suitable mesh assumptions, we establish parameter choices that retain the formal accuracy of the base discretization. Numerical experiments with summation-by-parts discretizations of the Burgers and Euler equations demonstrate substantially improved robustness for under-resolved flows and flows with shock waves while retaining high-order accuracy for smooth solutions, using the same parameter choices across several test problems. Overall, these results show that targeted dissipation can improve the robustness of high-order methods without excessive damping of resolved flow structures.

Researchers developed a new approach to artificial dissipation that adapts its strength and location based on the flow's behavior, aiming to improve robustness without sacrificing accuracy. fulltext.summary: The paper addresses the challenges of maintaining stability and accuracy in high-order numerical methods for solving partial differential equations. The authors introduce a novel framework for nonlinear artificial dissipation, inspired by residual correction methods, designed to be applied to summation-by-parts discretizations. This framework allows for controlled dissipation strength and spatial distribution, preserving discrete conservation and entropy stability while minimizing impact on accuracy, as demonstrated through numerical experiments on the Burgers and Euler equations. The method is element-local and discretization agnostic, with the artificial dissipation term constructed independently of the base spatial residual, and the authors establish parameter choices that retain the formal accuracy of the base discretization.

items.abstract: We establish a strong convergence rate for the implicit midpoint method applied to the periodic stochastic Korteweg-de Vries equation with additive noise, addressing a question that has remained open since the work of Debussche and Printems. To control nonlinear error growth, we obtain exponential integrability estimates for the exact and comparison solutions using the coercivity of a classical KdV invariant. We then derive local error bounds from estimates for the comparison solutions and control error accumulation through an $L^2$ error propagation identity that isolates a martingale increment. Under $H_0^{9/2}$ regularity assumptions on the noise and the deterministic initial data, we prove that, on every fixed finite time interval, the maximum $L^2(\mathbb{T})$ error at the time points is $O(h)$ in $L^p(Ω)$ for every $1\le p<\infty$. Notably, the exponential integrability and the convergence rate hold for every damping coefficient $λ\ge0$, including the undamped case $λ=0$. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted first-order convergence.

plain.summary: The study investigates the behavior of a specific numerical scheme for solving a nonlinear partial differential equation influenced by random fluctuations. Researchers developed refined mathematical tools to manage the effects of the nonlinearity and noise, ultimately leading to estimates on the error introduced by the numerical approximation. The analysis demonstrates that the error accumulates at a rate proportional to the step size, confirming a theoretical prediction through computational experiments. This result extends previous findings by providing a convergence analysis applicable even in the absence of damping.

items.title: Provable Method of Moments for Cryo-EM
items.abstract: We study the recovery of a three-dimensional volume in single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) from noisy tomographic projections acquired at unknown viewing rotations, drawn independently and uniformly from $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. We show that, in a spherical-shell representation satisfying an explicit shell-separation condition, the first three moments generically determine the underlying real volume up to its intrinsic global $\mathrm{O}(3)$ ambiguity. The proof is constructive and yields a frequency-marching procedure that successively recovers the volume. Consequently, consistent recovery in the high-noise regime has sample complexity $n=ω(σ^6)$, where $n$ is the number of observations and $σ^2$ is the noise variance. Numerical experiments validate the constructive recovery scheme under finite sampling and additive noise, and indicate that direct third-moment optimization can succeed beyond the structural assumptions required by the constructive proof.

plain.summary: The work addresses the reconstruction of a 3D volume from projections subject to rotational uncertainty and noise. A theoretical framework is developed based on the analysis of moments in a specific representation, demonstrating a relationship between these moments and the underlying volume. The authors provide a constructive recovery algorithm and derive a sample complexity bound dependent on the noise variance, which is then verified through numerical simulations.

fulltext.summary: The work addresses the problem of reconstructing a three-dimensional volume from noisy projections, where the projections are acquired at unknown rotations. A constructive recovery scheme is developed based on the first three moments in a spherical-shell representation, which recovers the volume up to an ambiguity. Numerical validation using synthetic volumes, such as TRPV1 and the 80S ribosome, demonstrates the effectiveness of the method, with forward-marched shells exhibiting a relative error of $1.39\times 10^{3}$ at $\ell=2$ and backfilled shells reaching $2.07\times 10^{8}$. The experiments also suggest favorable optimization behavior, with aligned errors agreeing to within $10^{-6}$ for the 80S ribosome at signal-to-noise ratios greater than or equal to 1.

items.abstract: Rayleigh-Bénard convection (RBC) is a model for turbulent flow and challenging to simulate by direct numerical simulation (DNS). Adequate resolution of all relevant length scales requires very fine grids in space and stability restrictions can dictate small step sizes. In this paper, we investigate the use of parallel spectral deferred correction (SDC) as a high-order time-stepping method to reduce wall-clock times of direct numerical simulation of RBC. Performance results on JUSUF (CPUs) and JUPITER (GPUs) with two different codes show parallel SDC can offer some concurrency along the temporal axis plus larger maximum stable time steps. Taken together, this allows for a reduction of wall-clock time required for simulations over one free-fall time by having to compute fewer steps and being able to mitigate the higher cost per time step through temporal parallelization.

Researchers employed a parallelized spectral deferred correction method to advance the solution in time, aiming to improve simulation efficiency. The implementation on both CPU and GPU architectures demonstrated the potential for reduced wall-clock time through increased temporal parallelism and larger stable time steps. These improvements collectively contribute to a faster overall simulation process.

fulltext.summary: The study addresses the computational challenges of simulating turbulent flow using direct numerical simulation (DNS), specifically focusing on Rayleigh-Bénard convection. Researchers implemented a parallel spectral deferred correction (SDC) method, a high-order time-stepping technique, to reduce simulation time by distributing computations across multiple processors. The implementation utilizes a diagonal approximation of a matrix and involves distributing the evaluation of the right-hand side and node solution updates across multiple processes, with a reported efficiency of approximately 80% for parallelized components. The authors demonstrate that this approach allows for a reduction in wall-clock time required for simulations, achieved through fewer time steps and leveraging temporal parallelization.

items.title: Neural Dimensional Analysis: Foundations of Dimensionless and Scale-Consistent Computation
items.abstract: Modern Transformers rely on many scale-control mechanisms, including normalization, residual scaling, attention temperatures, loss weighting, and adaptive updates. To explain how these mechanisms maintain scale consistency, we introduce Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), a unified framework based on dimensional consistency. We define neural units that specify how tensors rescale and which quantities can be added, just as physical units do in physics. Our rules match residual units, nondimensionalize attention and gate inputs, combine losses across units, and convert gradient units into parameter units. We implement NDA through dimensionless Unit Violation Indices (UVI) for diagnosing scale mismatches within Transformers, a unit-consistent multi-loss objective, and the Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) with normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions. In language-model experiments spanning 51M to 1B parameters, GCT remains stable during training across a broad sixteenfold learning-rate range, outperforming Pre-LN, LLaMA-style, and QK-Norm in 124M validation loss at tuned learning rates. GCT's normalized residual stream also shows improved robustness to quantization. At 1B parameters, calibrated per-tensor int8 quantization increases GCT's validation loss by only 0.009 nats, compared with up to 5.51 nats for the baselines. Vision and physics-informed neural network experiments further confirm NDA's benefits beyond language modeling. These results establish dimensional consistency as a neural network design principle.

plain.summary: The work investigates the principles behind scale consistency in Transformer architectures, drawing parallels to dimensional analysis in physics. A novel framework, Neural Dimensional Analysis (NDA), is proposed to define neural units and diagnose scale mismatches using Unit Violation Indices. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of their approach by developing a Gauge-Canonical Transformer (GCT) that exhibits improved training stability, robustness to quantization, and performance across various scales and tasks, including vision and physics-informed neural network applications.

Experiments with GCT, using normalized coordinates and orthogonalized residual additions, demonstrated improved training stability and robustness to quantization, achieving a 124M validation loss of 0.009 nats with int8 quantization at 1B parameters.

items.title: Numerical simulation of biological capsules based on interface-fitted polygonal meshes
items.abstract: In this work we introduce a numerical framework for the simulation of biological capsules based on meshes that adapt iteration-wise to the shape of the membrane. The discretization leverages a Hybrid High Order method (HHO) to solve a Stokes problem with a source term distributed on the interface between the internal and the external phases. The HHO discretization supports meshes composed of general polygons, permitting to use fitted meshes that can be easily generated by cutting the elements intersected by the interface. Moreover, polygonal meshes allow arbitrarily accurate interface discretizations without introducing bulk degrees of freedom. The presentation of the simulation algorithm is completed with a proof-of-concept numerical test on a well-established benchmark: the deformation of an elastic capsule immersed in a shear flow.

[Conclusion and Perspectives] In this work, we have proposed a novel approach for the simulation of capsule dynamics based on interface-fitted polygonal meshes, summarized in Algorithm 1. The methodology leverages a Hybrid High Order discretization for flow equations supporting polygonal meshes. The flexibility of the method in terms of mesh requirements allows to treat in a straightforward way the interface conditions associated to the fluid-structure interaction while keeping the overhead linked to mesh adaptation moderate. As a proof of concept, the performance of the polygonal interface-fitted approach has been tested successfully on a simple yet paradigmatic benchmark featuring a capsule undergoing moderate to strong deformation in shear flow.

plain.summary: The study addresses the computational modeling of deformable objects with distinct internal and external phases. A novel numerical method, termed Hybrid High Order (HHO), is employed to solve a fluid dynamics problem, with the interface between the phases represented by a polygonal mesh that dynamically adjusts during the simulation. This approach facilitates accurate representation of the interface without unnecessary computational overhead in the bulk fluid domain, demonstrated through a benchmark test involving capsule deformation.

fulltext.summary: The work addresses the simulation of deformable objects by adapting a mesh to the object's boundary. A Hybrid High Order (HHO) method is used to solve a Stokes problem on a mesh composed of general polygons, allowing for accurate interface discretization and easy mesh generation. The approach was validated through a test case involving the deformation of an elastic capsule immersed in a shear flow, demonstrating accurate reproduction of the capsule's trajectory and achieving results comparable to existing methods.

items.title: Conformalized Physics-Informed Weak Regression for Parameter Estimation in Epidemic Models
items.abstract: Compartment models of infectious diseases are often linear in coefficients that are physical parameters or products or ratios of them. We exploit this with closed-form least squares and equip the estimates with distribution-free uncertainty. Physics-informed regression (PIR) fits the parameters to finite-difference derivatives of the data; we introduce physics-informed weak regression (PIWR), which integrates the model in time instead, needs no derivatives of the data, estimates the initial state jointly and is high-order accurate. To quantify uncertainty we wrap both estimators in split conformal prediction, with a calibration population generated by the physics-based model itself, giving simultaneous intervals for all parameters with a finite-sample coverage guarantee. A residual-adaptive factor, computed without ground truth, scales the intervals to each data set (PIWR-RACC). On the eleven benchmark models of disease-informed neural networks (DINNs), PIWR or PIR-FD6 is one to four orders of magnitude more accurate than the reported DINN results wherever the sampling resolves the dynamics, in about a millisecond per fit instead of minutes to hours of training, and the 90% intervals achieve 87-92% coverage in all 88 settings. On the S3I3R model of the original PIR study, PIWR lowers the reported PIR errors by about three orders of magnitude. On real data from the 1978 boarding-school influenza outbreak, a variable-projection variant gives calibrated 95% intervals that overlap those of a Bayesian analysis. On a time-varying transmission benchmark, a B-spline expansion of beta(t) keeps PIR and PIWR linear; they are more accurate than physics-informed neural networks in three of four cases and comparable in the noisiest, with simultaneous bands for beta(t). The complete conformal calibration takes less than two minutes for every benchmark.

plain.summary: The study addresses the challenge of accurately estimating parameters within mathematical models of disease spread, particularly when these parameters are related through physical constraints. The researchers developed a novel method, physics-informed weak regression (PIWR), which integrates the model over time to estimate parameters and initial states without requiring derivatives of the data. Results demonstrate significantly improved accuracy and efficiency compared to existing methods, including disease-informed neural networks, alongside the generation of calibrated uncertainty intervals for all parameters.

fulltext.summary: The study addresses the estimation of parameters within a system of differential equations describing epidemic dynamics. A regression framework is developed where the model's time derivative is expressed as a function of state variables and a set of physical parameters, with the initial condition also treated as an unknown. The method, termed Physics-informed Weak Regression (PIWR), integrates the model in time and jointly estimates the initial state, achieving high-order accuracy and providing distribution-free uncertainty quantification through conformal prediction. The approach demonstrates improved accuracy and efficiency compared to physics-informed neural networks, particularly in time-varying transmission scenarios, with the constant beta recovered to 6*10^-5.

items.title: Beyond Time Induction: Structured Conditional Neural Solvers for Parametric Stochastic-Volatility Pricing
items.abstract: Physics-informed neural networks provide a flexible framework for learning parametric PDE solution families without labeled data, yet preserving accurate derivatives across heterogeneous regimes remains challenging. Structured neural solvers offer compact representations, but restrictive conditional parameterizations can limit adaptation across the solution family. We introduce BeTINN, a structured conditional architecture extending time-induced modulation through multi-directional time-parameter conditioning and a joint residual pathway. We evaluate BeTINN on the Heston stochastic-volatility PDE, a demanding parametric problem with mixed derivatives and economically relevant first- and second-order sensitivities. BeTINN improves joint accuracy across normalized option value and key sensitivity metrics relative to our baselines. Controlled ablations characterize the roles of its architectural components. We further find that validation physics loss is informative but does not fully determine differential fidelity, and that accurate solution values can coexist with localized derivative errors. These results support structured conditional adaptation and motivate derivative-aware evaluation when sensitivities are downstream quantities of interest.

plain.summary: The study addresses the challenge of efficiently and accurately solving parametric partial differential equations using neural networks. Researchers developed a novel architecture, BeTINN, which combines structured neural solvers with a flexible conditioning mechanism to improve performance on a complex stochastic-volatility pricing problem. The method demonstrates enhanced accuracy in both solution values and sensitivities compared to existing approaches, while also highlighting the importance of evaluating derivative fidelity independently of solution accuracy. The findings contribute to understanding the interplay between architecture design and solution quality in physics-informed neural networks.

fulltext.summary: The work addresses the challenge of accurately solving parametric partial differential equations, specifically focusing on the Heston stochastic-volatility model used for option pricing. Researchers developed BeTINN, a structured conditional neural network architecture that extends time-induced modulation to improve derivative accuracy across different solution regimes. Evaluations on the Heston model demonstrated improved accuracy in both option values and sensitivities compared to baseline methods, while also revealing a disconnect between validation physics loss and derivative fidelity. The study highlights the importance of derivative-aware evaluation when sensitivities are critical outputs.

items.abstract: We study a spherical perfectly matched layer (PML) method for the time-harmonic Maxwell scattering problem with large wavenumber. Using vector spherical harmonics and a modal transformation for the coupled transverse magnetic components, we establish the sharp wavenumber-explicit stability estimate for the truncated PML problem and prove that its inf-sup constant is of order $O(κ^{-1})$. We then analyze the first-order Nédélec edge element method and its continuous interior penalty counterpart. Under the condition that $κ^3h^2$ is sufficiently small, the preasymptotic errors in the energy norm and the $κ$-scaled $\mathbf{L}^2$ norm are of orders $O(κh+κ^3h^2)$ and $O(κ^2h^2+κ^3h^2)$, respectively. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical results.

plain.summary: The work addresses the challenge of simulating electromagnetic wave propagation using a specialized boundary condition technique. Researchers developed a spherical perfectly matched layer method, employing mathematical transformations to ensure stability and control the accuracy of the solution. The analysis focuses on the behavior of the method as the wave number increases, revealing the relationship between the wave number and the discretization size for achieving accurate results, which were validated through computational experiments.

fulltext.summary: The paper investigates a spherical perfectly matched layer (PML) method for solving time-harmonic Maxwell scattering problems with large wavenumbers. The method utilizes vector spherical harmonics and a modal transformation to derive stability estimates and analyze the inf-sup constant, which is of order $O(κ^{-1})$. Numerical experiments using the Nédélec edge element method and its continuous interior penalty counterpart demonstrate preasymptotic errors in the energy norm and the $κ$-scaled $\mathbf{L}^2$ norm of orders $O(κh+κ^3h^2)$ and $O(κ^2h^2+κ^3h^2)$, respectively, with the condition that $κ^3h^2$ is sufficiently small. items.title: Sequential Learning-Based Physics-Informed Neural Network Modeling for Parameter Estimation on a Power Converter
items.abstract: A staged physics-informed neural network (PINN) is proposed for identifying the inductance, capacitance and parasitic resistances of a DC buck converter from time-domain data. Gradients are released in the order of L to C to rL to rC, a sequence derived from sensitivity analysis. The five-stage schedule recovers L and C to within 5% and the series ESR to 10%, while a three-stage variant attains the same accuracy 11% faster. An 84 factorial sweep confirms that the trained PINN remains accurate for simultaneous 8% perturbations of all four components, achieving a waveform RMSE of 2.6 x 10-2 over 5 ms-an order-of-magnitude better than a simultaneous-training baseline.

plain.summary: The study addresses the challenge of accurately determining component parameters in a power converter using limited data. A novel architecture, termed a sequential learning-based PINN, is developed to iteratively estimate inductance, capacitance, and parasitic resistances. The method employs a staged release of gradients, guided by sensitivity analysis, to improve the convergence and accuracy of the parameter estimation process. Results demonstrate a significant improvement in estimation accuracy and training speed compared to a conventional simultaneous training approach, validated through a comprehensive parameter perturbation analysis.

fulltext.summary: The study addresses parameter identification in a DC buck converter using a physics-informed neural network. A sequential training approach is implemented, releasing gradients for inductance, capacitance, and parasitic resistances in a specific order determined by sensitivity analysis. The resulting model achieves an accuracy of 5% for inductance and capacitance, and 10% for series ESR, with a faster training time compared to a simultaneous training method.
